query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, minor addition of reactive elements (e.g., yttrium and hafnium) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its operational stability under extreme temperature cycling, long-term loading (creep), and corrosive environments without sacrificing its strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy produced via conventional casting that exhibits a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a small concentration (e.g., ~1–2 atomic percent total) of grain-boundary‐active elements such as Y and Hf during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Tested under cyclic thermal fluctuations (up to ~700°C), long-term mechanical loading (to assess room-temperature and elevated-temperature creep), and in corrosive media (such as saline or chloride-containing environments typical of aircraft/space fastener service).
generation.structural_mediator: The trace additions are expected to segregate preferentially to grain boundaries and phase interfaces, leading to enhanced boundary stability and the formation of protective oxide phases that are adherent and slow further degradation.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf atoms at the phase boundaries stabilize the microstructure by retarding grain coarsening and dislocation motion, enhance the formation of continuous, low-energy oxide films during exposure to high temperatures or corrosive conditions, and thereby reduce creep rates and corrosion-induced damage without hindering the intrinsic strength–ductility synergy of the lamellar structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should display improved creep resistance, enhanced thermal and corrosion stability under service conditions, and maintained (or possibly slightly improved) tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
generation.baseline: The current performance of as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with its inherited lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, which, while having a good strength–ductility balance, shows limitations in long-term creep and corrosion resistance under cyclic high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated when the added elements are within a narrow doping range (approximately 1–2 at.%), and the processing remains compatible with the alloy’s eutectic solidification. Excessive additions or incompatible processing might result in undesirable second phases or loss of ductility.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in creep rate reduction and corrosion resistance have not been established; the optimum concentration and process adjustments require experimental validation. There is also uncertainty regarding whether the grain-boundary segregation will fully offset any potential embrittlement or other negative impacts at very high service temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 samples: one set with 1–2 at.% combined Y and Hf additions introduced during melting/casting, and a control set without these additions. Subject both sets to (a) cyclic thermal tests (heating and cooling cycles up to 700°C), (b) long-term creep tests at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, and (c) corrosion tests in a simulated chloride or saline environment. Microstructural evolution should be monitored via TEM/SEM and phase analysis via XRD.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves at relevant temperatures
Corrosion rates (using weight loss and electrochemical impedance methods)
Tensile strength and ductility (stress-strain measurements) before and after testing
Microstructural stability (grain size, phase boundary integrity as observed by TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y/Hf-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in creep resistance and corrosion performance compared to the control, or if its strength–ductility balance degrades (e.g., reduced ductility or increased embrittlement) after thermal cycling, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively. As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
